Kit

kit/net: replication core

31 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Replication lanesDeclaring a replicated entityCommand consequencesComposing verbs from embedded blocksWire codecsDynamic collectionsField-change edgesAdvanced: registry primitivesThe per-tick walksAdvanced: the command-loop primitivesTyped app messagesWire, tick, and clocksThe two timelines (presenting consequences)Shared replication and simulation primitivesConstraints and failure cases

kit/net implements Kit's engine-independent wire primitives, entity registry, field descriptors, reliable delta replication, owner streams, interpolation, and command prediction. It does not import Godot and is covered by headless tests.

Most game code uses these mechanisms through kit/session, which drives the registry and schedules messages. Import kit/net directly for types such as Net_Id and Player_Id, wire readers and writers, custom interpolation procedures, clocks, and low-level tests. kit/netgd provides the Godot transport adapter.

Replication lanes#

Session replication has two field lanes:

  • Reliable deltas are selected by gd:"replicate". The host writes shared state such as inventory, health, score, and match phase. Changes are delivered reliably.
  • Owner streams are selected by gd:"owner". The current entity owner writes freshness-oriented state such as movement and aim. The host checks the sender's ownership and relays accepted samples; other peers interpolate them.

The lanes are disjoint in the generated descriptor. A full spawn or resync record sets their initial values, after which only the selected lane updates each field. Owner streams trust the owner to provide their values. Use kit/sim when the authority must derive contested state from inputs; see Choosing an authority model.

Delta replication#

Each registered entity has a shadow copy of its reliable fields. At every network tick, the registry compares current values with that shadow, writes a field mask and the changed values for dirty entities, and advances the shadow. Unchanged entities emit no field data.

Replicated fields must have a bounded, target-independent wire shape. The normal building blocks are fixed-width scalars (i32, not int), explicitly based enums (enum u8, not bare enum; explicit member values are integer literals), literal-sized arrays, and recursively valid structs. A raw struct may contain no compiler-owned interior or tail padding; reorder its fields, add explicit reserved bytes, or deliberately use struct #packed. Pointers, strings, and dynamic containers do not belong in replicated fields; send variable-length data with application messages, entity blobs, or kit/xfer.

Canonical wire ABI#

scriptgen recursively validates every Kit-owned raw network value: replicated, owner-streamed, and predicted fields; input records; player profiles; and typed app-message payloads. It follows fixed arrays, aliases, distinct types, explicit enums, nested structs, imported package types, and composed blocks all the way to their leaves. It rejects int, uint, uintptr, implicit-width enums, pointers, strings, dynamic or fixed-capacity containers, unresolved types, and implicit struct padding. Custom field codecs still require a recursively valid in-memory value and a literal fixed codec size.

The generated guard exposes the wire schema, its hashes, and structured metadata for the package:

Odin
NET_SCHEMA_CANONICAL  // readable, deterministic wire metadata
NET_ABI_FINGERPRINT   // hash of that metadata alone
NET_FINGERPRINT       // complete session contract, including the ABI
NET_SCHEMA            // knet.Net_Schema: structured, allocation-free metadata

The canonical schema records full field paths, wire kinds, struct and packet widths, array and protocol bounds, enum bases and values, input-class ids and admission constraints, message tags, and each action's access, prediction, argument ceiling, and immediate/tick scheduling. Generated size_of, align_of, and field-layout assertions check those expectations in every target compile. The raw ABI is little-endian; a target with a different layout cannot retain the same accepted fingerprint.

NET_SCHEMA exposes that metadata to tools and diagnostics. It contains flat static tables for entity kinds, recursive type nodes, replicated fields, input classes and constraints, actions, presentation events, argument layouts, outcome layouts, profiles, and typed messages. Each action carries its resolved Action_Policy, .Immediate/.Scheduled model, argument/outcome spans, and named consequence metadata; each presentation event carries its named anchor and watch-clock schedule. The schema also carries both fingerprints and the exact canonical string that produced NET_ABI_FINGERPRINT.

Rows with children use knet.Net_Schema_Span indexes into the schema's backing tables, so inspection allocates nothing. Common lookups have helpers:

Odin
assert(knet.net_schema_valid(&NET_SCHEMA))
field, ok := knet.net_schema_field(&NET_SCHEMA, "Runner", "position")
action, ok := knet.net_schema_action(&NET_SCHEMA, "Chest", "open")
if ok {
	args := knet.net_schema_action_args(&NET_SCHEMA, action)
	outcomes := knet.net_schema_action_outcomes(&NET_SCHEMA, action)
	// policy, model, args/outcomes, consequence, widths, and bounds are authoritative.
}

Treat generated schema tables as read-only. Executable callbacks and live entity pointers stay in the runtime descriptors; NET_SCHEMA contains stable protocol facts only, so it is safe to expose to diagnostics, compatibility tools, and future admission/configuration APIs without creating another registry.

Use explicit bytes when alignment would otherwise create a hole:

Odin
Stage :: struct {
	run:      u16,
	level:    u8,
	reserved: u8, // protocol data, unlike invisible tail padding
}

Formatting and comments do not move the fingerprint. A wire type, bound, policy, schedule, or codec name/size does. If a custom codec's meaning changes without changing its declared name or size, rename/version it or mix a semantic contract with session_mix_fingerprint; code bodies are not schema data.

Commands#

A command is a proc marked @(gd_command) whose return value says whether its mutation applied. The bare marker is owner-only and waits for authority state. A typed Action_Policy preset enables prediction or widens access. Script generation creates the decoder, policy descriptor, stable command ID, and typed <verb>_cmd wrapper.

The common policies are:

Declaration Access Client execution
bare @(gd_command) (its resolved policy is knet.ACTION_OWNER) owner waits for authority state
knet.ACTION_OWNER_PREDICTED owner optimistic
knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT any playing seat waits for authority state
knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT_PREDICTED any playing seat optimistic when that peer has a prediction ledger
knet.ACTION_AUTHORITY authority only never crosses client ingress

Access and prediction are independent of the command predicate. The authority checks the playing seat and access rule before executing gameplay code. Co-op and sim actions consume one generated Action_Desc(Id) containing the stable id, execution model, policy, typed argument/outcome metadata, and consequence metadata. Only the callback differs: Command_Desc adds immediate invocation, while Sim_Cmd adds scheduled exec/apply thunks. Moving a verb between models does not duplicate or reinterpret its declaration.

To set a smaller encoded-argument limit, use the typed literal form. Zero uses the 4096-byte default; a positive value is enforced before client send and again at authority ingress:

Odin
@(gd_command = knet.Action_Policy {
	access         = .Any_Seat,
	prediction     = .Optimistic,
	max_args_bytes = 64,
})

Quoted command-policy strings are rejected. Use a typed preset or literal so the compiler can check policy members.

A successful command may invoke a name-paired <verb>_then half for authority-only cross-entity work such as spawning, crediting a player, or transferring ownership.

For an optimistic command:

  • confirmation retains the optimistic mutation;
  • predicate rejection includes authoritative entity state rather than restoring a possibly stale local snapshot; admission failures send a compact result and restore the local capture while ordinary replication supplies newer state;
  • timeout reverts an action whose result never arrives; and
  • an intervening authoritative update unwinds pending predictions, applies that state, and replays still-valid commands in issue order.

The generated wrapper takes ^kboot.Boot so the call site is the same for a session command and a tick-scheduled simulation command:

Odin
outcome := chest_take_cmd(&game.boot, chest, slot, px, py)
if knet.command_ok(outcome) {show_local_take_feedback()}
if outcome.reason == .Access {show_locked_feedback()}

The wrapper returns Action_Outcome:

Odin
Action_Outcome :: struct {
	state:  Command_Outcome,       // Applied, Predicted, or Rejected
	reason: Action_Reject_Reason,  // None unless this call refused locally
	seq:    u32,                   // correlates the final callback
	model:  Action_Model,          // Immediate or Scheduled
}

For session replication, .Applied means the local authority accepted the command. .Predicted means an issue is in flight or scheduled. .Rejected means it did not apply locally. command_ok accepts the detailed outcome, so ordinary call sites remain one condition. Inspect reason only where the UI cares why a synchronous refusal occurred.

The authority's eventual answer is delivered through the generated session halves. Both immediate and tick-scheduled actions use these same callbacks:

Odin
@(gd_half)
game_command_rejected :: proc(
	self: ^Game,
	seq: knet.Intent_Seq,
	entity: knet.Net_Id,
	cmd: u16,
	reason: knet.Action_Reject_Reason,
	model: knet.Action_Model,
) {
	switch reason {
	case .Access:    show_locked_feedback()
	case .Rate:      show_slow_down_feedback()
	case .Predicate: show_no_longer_available()
	case .Timeout:   show_connection_feedback()
	case:            // Malformed/Stale are normally logged, not player choices.
	}
}

Action_Reject_Reason groups failures by the response a game may need to show:

Reason Meaning
Access The seat or action policy did not allow the request.
Rate The shared traffic budget or scheduled-action queue refused it.
Malformed Unknown action, invalid/trailing encoding, or argument envelope failure.
Stale The target, sequence, or requested scheduling window is no longer current.
Predicate The authored command proc returned false.
Timeout No final authority result arrived before the safety horizon.

game_command_confirmed receives (seq, entity, cmd, model). On the authority, game_command_executed receives (player, entity, cmd, reason, seq, model) for both execution models. The generated callbacks handle verdict decoding and sequence tracking. model disambiguates the two sequence/id namespaces when a game uses both. Non-predicted actions keep a receipt-only entry, so they confirm, reject, and time out through exactly the same callback path without gaining speculative write privileges.

A purchase dialog, transaction prompt, or similar UI may need the final verdict for one particular action. Turn the generated outcome into a session-scoped receipt and poll it from the frame loop:

Odin
outcome := spelunker_buy_cmd(&game.boot, game.me, ITEM_BOOTS)
receipt := ksess.session_action_receipt(&game.ses, outcome)

// A later frame:
if verdict, ready := ksess.session_action_poll(&game.ses, receipt); ready {
	switch verdict.state {
	case .Accepted:    close_purchase_dialog()
	case .Rejected:    show_purchase_error(verdict.reason)
	case .Unavailable: show_connection_error()
	case .Pending:     // `ready` is false for this state
	}
}

Receipts are optional and bounded (MAX_ACTION_RECEIPTS, 64 watched actions per run). Polling a final result releases its watched slot; call session_action_forget when the owning UI disappears first. They cover both .Immediate and .Scheduled actions without aliasing equal raw sequences and preserve the typed rejection reason. A pending watched receipt becomes .Unavailable across reset/rehost. A small result cache closes the issue/result race for synchronous in-memory transports.

A receipt acknowledges the action's result. Durable inventory, currency, ownership, and world state still come from replicated fields and their change callbacks. A receipt uses the existing action result and creates no additional request/response protocol or wire message.

Generated command IDs are stable hashes of command names, not declaration positions. Reordering procedures does not renumber the protocol. Renaming a command intentionally creates a new ID; collisions within a command set are a build error. The session's schema fingerprint provides the broader compatibility gate.

Reliable presentation events#

@(gd_event) declares a typed, non-durable occurrence. The author keeps the presentation body under _fx; scriptgen generates an announcement procedure with the suffix removed, taking the game's ^Boot:

Odin
@(gd_event = "audience=everyone,timing=auto")
chest_spark_fx :: proc(g: ^Game, chest: ^Chest, mine: bool, strength: f32) {
	particles_restart(chest, strength)
	if mine {camera_kick(g)}
}

// Announce the event from authority gameplay code.
chest_spark(&g.boot, chest, 0.8)

The signature is (game, entity refs…, mine: bool, wire args…), with the game pointer first. One entity parameter is the inferred anchor; with several, write anchor=PARAM, or anchor=none for a world occurrence. Arguments after mine use the command wire primitives. The body returns nothing and is presentation only. Use commands, authority steps, and replicated fields for damage, inventory, spawning, and other durable gameplay state.

The policy has two independent axes:

  • audience=everyone presents on every eligible screen.
  • audience=owner presents only on the anchor owner's screen and therefore requires an anchor.
  • audience=observers excludes the anchor owner. With no anchor it excludes the announcing authority, useful when the source already carries its effect.
  • timing=immediate presents from the next session-frame drain on receivers.
  • timing=anchored aligns non-owning screens with the anchor's presentation clock; the owning/live screen receives no additional interpolation delay.
  • timing=auto is accepted only when scriptgen can prove the clock: a sim-tracked anchor uses its watch clock, and a cooperative entity with continuous owner state uses the session interpolation clock. An anchorless event in a lane-owning game uses that lane's watch clock. Other static and custom clocks must say immediate or use the lower-level explicit scheduler.

The anchor also determines which transport implementation carries the event. A sim-tracked anchor uses SIM_FACT; a cooperative/static event uses the session's reliable event frame and presentation queue. Both enter the wire fingerprint with id, argument schema, anchor, audience, and timing. Neither is join-replayed. Cooperative/static events are authority-minted; clients ask through commands. A sim event may also present from the owning live pass, where it is derived from the same replayable tick rather than an unconfirmed standalone prediction.

@(gd_event) is the sole declaration for presentation events. Tick _fx, field _edge, command _then, and resimulation _apply callbacks still run in their respective phases.

Network tick and interpolation#

For session replication, the fixed network tick (20 Hz by default) schedules deltas and streams; ordinary gameplay may still run at frame rate. Remote owner streams render at interp_delay, normally far enough behind the newest sample to interpolate between two values. If no newer sample exists, presentation holds the latest value instead of extrapolating indefinitely.

Declaring a replicated entity#

Tag fields and mark procedures so scriptgen can emit the descriptor. The owner: gd.Node2d field below holds the Godot node; it is separate from the network entity owner that controls write access. This example comes from examples/cavecrawl/scripts/chest.odin:

Odin
Chest :: struct {
	owner:  gd.Node2d,
	net_id: knet.Net_Id,
	x, y:   f32 `gd:"replicate"`,
	slots:  [8]kitems.Slot `gd:"replicate"`,
}

@(gd_command = knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT_PREDICTED)
chest_take :: proc(self: ^Chest, slot: i32, px: f32, py: f32) -> (ok: bool, taken: kitems.Slot) {
	if !kinter.in_range({px, py, 0}, {self.x, self.y, 0}, REACH) {return false, {}}
	taken = kitems.take(self.slots[:], int(slot), 99) // the whole stack
	return taken.count > 0, taken
}

// After acceptance, the authority runs this cross-entity consequence.
@(gd_half)
chest_take_then :: proc(game: ^CaveLobby, self: ^Chest, by: knet.Player_Id, slot: i32, px: f32, py: f32, taken: kitems.Slot) {
	cave_credit(game, by, self, taken)
}

Owner-streamed float/vector/quaternion fields interpolate by default: x, y: f32 gd:"owner"`` (the spelunker's position). Discrete owner fields snap to the received value; write snap when a float field, such as a generation counter or meter, should also update without interpolation. The generated descriptor uses these types:

Odin
Field_Desc :: struct {
	offset: uintptr,
	size:   int,
	flags:  Field_Flags,
	lerp:   Lerp_Kind, // how stream sampling blends this field (meaningful with .Interp)
	blend:  Blend_Proc, // required iff lerp == .Custom
	wire:   Wire_Kind, // how the field's bytes are encoded in packets (default: raw)
	codec:  Wire_Codec, // required iff wire == .Custom
}

Entity_Desc :: struct {
	fields: []Field_Desc,
}

Action_Policy :: struct {
	access:         Action_Access,
	prediction:     Action_Prediction,
	max_args_bytes: int,
}

Action_Desc :: struct($Id: typeid) {
	name:        string,
	id:          Id,
	model:       Action_Model,
	policy:      Action_Policy,
	arguments:   []Action_Argument_Desc,
	outcomes:    []Action_Outcome_Value_Desc,
	consequence: Action_Consequence_Desc,
}

Command_Desc :: struct {
	using action: Action_Desc(Cmd_Id),
	invoke:       Command_Proc,
}

Command_Set :: struct {
	entity_desc:   ^Entity_Desc,
	commands:      []Command_Desc,
	net_id_offset: int,
}

At most MAX_REPLICATED_FIELDS :: 64 fields per entity (the dirty mask is one u64; a fixed array counts as one field). Lerp_Kind covers .Snap, .F32, .F64, .Quat (nlerp with hemisphere flip), .Angle (f32 radians blending the shortest arc, declared heading: f32 `gd:"owner,interp=angle"`; a raw lerp from +3.1 to -3.1 sweeps the long way around), and .Custom with an author-supplied Blend_Proc :: proc(dst, a, b: rawptr, alpha: f32) (declared via tint: [3]f32 `gd:"owner,interp=blend_oklab"`).

Command consequences#

A command proc may mutate only its target entity, which is the state covered by prediction and reconciliation. Put cross-entity work in the name-paired <verb>_then half. Script generation passes it the issuer, command arguments, and any returned payload after the command applies on the authority. Two signatures are supported:

Odin
@(gd_half) chest_take_then :: proc(game: ^CaveLobby, self: ^Chest, by: knet.Player_Id, slot: i32, px: f32, py: f32, taken: kitems.Slot)
@(gd_half) door_toggle_then :: proc(self: ^Door, by: knet.Player_Id)   // entity-local: no game param

A command may return (bool, payloads…). Results after the applied bool are in-process values passed directly to _then; they never cross the wire. Payload types are unconstrained, and the compiler checks them against the _then signature at the generated call site.

When a predicate needs the issuing player, declare by: knet.Player_Id right after the receiver, or after the wielder parameter in a composed block. The framework supplies ctx.me during the issuing peer's optimistic run and the resolved sender on the host. _then receives the same value.

Use this parameter when a trade needs to identify the confirming player or a first-come claim needs to record its claimant. The issuer is never a wire argument, so a client cannot forge it to confirm the other player's part of a trade by changing a supplied side: u8 value. See the trade recipe. The name is reserved: a wire argument called by is a build error. A player the command targets remains ordinary wire data under another name, such as who or target.

Odin
@(gd_command = knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT_PREDICTED)
trade_confirm :: proc(self: ^Trade, by: knet.Player_Id) -> (ok: bool, sealed: bool)

A consequence runs once per applied command, including commands issued by the host through the wrapper's authority branch. It never runs on a client's optimistic run, a registry replay, a rejection, or a deduped retransmit. It runs before the result is sent and before the tick's delta comparison, so its mutations reach every peer in the same batch as the command's own. The game parameter is the session game pointer installed through session_set_factory.

For an embedded block, pair the consequence with the generated command name. For example, weapon: play.Gun exposes gun_fire as runner_weapon_fire, which pairs with runner_weapon_fire_then. The block implements the target mutation and its state machine. The game handles accepted cross-entity changes in _then, without dispatching on a block index or entity type. The block can return a payload describing its result, such as a round being fired. A game that does not consume the payload declares no _then.

Scriptgen validates a consequence's parameters ([game,] self, by, wire args…, payload…) against the command. Every half must carry @(gd_half) to declare that it is intended to pair. If it has no matching command, scriptgen reports an error and lists the class's valid pairing names. Rename the procedure, or remove the attribute if it is not intended as a half.

The name decides what a half pairs with; the attribute declares only that pairing was intended. Both a wrong prefix (chest_taek_then) and a wrong suffix (chest_take_after) are build errors. A proc that merely ends in _then and never claimed to be a half is nothing special. A direct verb whose payload nobody consumes still produces a warning. For handlers that apply to commands regardless of their type, such as metrics, receipts, or replays, use the untyped command hook. The generated _then dispatch runs through the same authority path.

A command's prediction and reconciliation cover one target entity. They cannot capture, restore on rejection, or replay changes across multiple entities, such as a trade that modifies both players' bags. Make the transaction itself the target; see the mediating-entity recipe.

Composing verbs from embedded blocks#

An entity can embed a struct containing replicated fields and commands. A gd:"replicate" field inside the embedded struct joins the containing entity's descriptor at the combined field offset. A @(gd_command) procedure whose receiver is the embedded struct joins that entity's generated command table. This lets the block define its state and target mutations while each game defines the cross-entity consequences.

Both import spellings work: import play "godot:play" (the idiomatic alias) and a bare import "godot:play": scriptgen resolves a bare import by reading the target's package clause, so the embed composes either way.

Declare the verb on the block, embed the block, and the entity gets the command:

Odin
Gun :: struct {
	ammo:      u8 `gd:"replicate"`,
	state:     Gun_State `gd:"replicate"`, // a replicated FSM is a plain enum field + an edge half
	reload_cd: u16 `gd:"replicate"`,
}

// The receiver is the embedded Gun. An optional second pointer parameter
// receives the containing entity for access to its stats or cooldowns.
// This pointer is supplied locally; only the following arguments cross the wire.
@(gd_command = knet.ACTION_OWNER_PREDICTED)
gun_fire :: proc(g: ^Gun, owner: ^Runner, dx, dy: f32) -> bool { ... }

Runner :: struct {
	owner:  gd.Node2d,
	net_id: knet.Net_Id,
	weapon: Gun,   // -> the entity gets `runner_weapon_fire`
}

The entity's generated command name includes the field path. Two blocks of the same type therefore get distinct names and command IDs: weapon: Gun and sidearm: Gun become runner_weapon_fire and runner_sidearm_fire. Issue the command through runner_weapon_fire_cmd(&boot, self, dx, dy). The generated call supplies the containing entity, so the wrapper takes only the wire arguments after self.

Prediction rollback and authoritative rejection snapshots cover the block's replicated state because it is part of the entity's descriptor. Put cross-entity effects, such as spawning a projectile or applying damage, in the game's runner_weapon_fire_then consequence.

A block may optionally take a pointer to its containing entity as its second parameter. Scriptgen detects this from the signature: use ^Runner for a game-specific block or ^$E for a library block reused across entity types. For a block imported from another godot: package, the generated file imports that package and qualifies the call, such as play.gun_fire.

Here Runner names the game's character script. The optional containing-entity pointer is separate from both its Godot node and its network entity owner.

godot:play provides composed Gun, Ability, Channel, Health, and Telegraph blocks. The block owns its replicated state and any declared command; the game owns cadence, world validation, presentation, and cross-entity effects where those cannot be generalized. See the godot:play reference and the source headers under play/ for each block's exact contract.

A block's @(gd_method) or @(gd_rpc) procedure also joins the containing entity's method table. For example, gear_level on a gear: Gear field becomes robot_gear_level in generated code and is registered as gear_level with Godot. The generated trampoline passes &self.gear and supplies the containing entity if the signature requests it. An embedded block can therefore expose state, commands, methods, and RPCs to the appropriate //gd: interfaces, including GDScript and the editor.

Wire codecs#

A field codec changes the packet representation while preserving the struct's in-memory representation. Shadows, change detection, prediction capture and restore, and stream rings all hold struct-layout bytes. The writer encodes them for transmission, and the reader decodes them before applying state. A smaller wire representation can reduce bandwidth without changing comparison or rollback behavior.

gd:"replicate,...,wire=f16" sends f32 elements as half floats: half the bytes, ~3 significant digits, integers exact to 2048. Cavecrawl's spelunker and relic positions use this encoding. For another representation, declare a fixed-size custom codec as you would a blend procedure:

Odin
hp: i32 `gd:"replicate,wire=spelunker_hp_codec"` // encode the 0..100 range with the declared codec

spelunker_hp_codec :: knet.Wire_Codec {
	size   = 1,
	encode = proc(wire, field: rawptr) {(^u8)(wire)^ = u8(clamp((^i32)(field)^, 0, 255))},
	decode = proc(field, wire: rawptr) {(^i32)(field)^ = i32((^u8)(wire)^)},
}

Each field's encoded size must be fixed. Within that size, a codec can quantize values, pack bits, or send an index into a table that both peers build deterministically from a shared seed. The receiver can then reconstruct the entry without receiving its contents.

decode(encode(x)) should be stable because receivers retain decoded values; an unstable round trip can produce small corrections when predictions are confirmed. Change detection still compares struct bytes, so a change smaller than the wire precision still causes a send. Choose enough precision to represent changes that affect gameplay.

Dynamic collections#

A [dynamic]T, slice, or map tagged gd:"replicate" is a build error. Replication compares each field's bytes with a shadow, records changes in one bit of a u64 mask, and copies the received bytes into the corresponding field. A dynamic container's header refers to separately allocated elements, so copying the header cannot replicate its contents. Byte comparison also has no element identity: inserting an element at the front of an encoded collection changes every following position. Choose a representation according to the collection's size and update pattern:

  • For a bounded collection, use a fixed array with a count or sentinel, such as cavecrawl's bag: [6]kitems.Slot with ITEM_NONE for empty slots. The array is one replicated field, so change callbacks and prediction rollback cover the whole value. Choose and enforce the inventory bound in game code.
  • For text or authored bytes that change rarely, use an entity blob. Game code marks it dirty, and the session reliably sends the whole value and includes it in snapshots. This supplies the value to late joiners and to backups and saves that include the entity. Cavecrawl's floor inscription is an example.
  • For a live collection of independently changing objects, make each element an entity. Spawn inserts an element, despawn removes it, and replication compares each element's fields. Interest management selects which entities a peer receives, and late joiners receive the current relevant set. Cavecrawl represents each floor pickup as a Pickup entity with its own x/y/item/count and typed pickup_spawn, rather than storing pickups: [dynamic]Pickup on the level.

The build error lists these alternatives at the field. (gd:"backup" still accepts [dynamic]/map: the backup codec restores whole values on one peer; it never diffs across the wire.)

Field-change edges#

Deltas carry current values. To react to a change with a hurt flash, goal horn, or floor fanfare, declare a procedure named for the field and mark it @(gd_half). The session's per-frame change comparison passes it the old and new values:

Odin
// ([game,] self, old, new: <the field's declared type>) — no results
@(gd_half)
gunner_hp_edge :: proc(self: ^Gunner, old, new: i32) {
	if new < old {self.flash_ttl = 0.25}
}

The change comparison follows these rules:

  • A half runs at most once per frame for the net change. A predicting client may write a reliable-delta field several times through optimistic execution, authoritative rejection state, and reconciliation replay. The half runs only if the final value differs from the previous frame's value.
  • A tagged POD struct or fixed array counts as one field. Group values in one struct when the callback must receive them together. Speedball's score: Score groups l, r, and won, so one callback receives the complete old and new score for each goal.
  • Equal values produce no callback. A 1→0→1 pulse inside one frame has no net change, and resetting from level 1 to level 1 changes no bytes. To represent a reset, include a generation counter in the same field: stage: struct { run: u16, level: u8, reserved: u8 }. Increment run on a reset and test old.run != new.run for cleanup. This records same-level resets and within-frame round trips. A late joiner receives run = 5 as its initial value and replays zero previous resets. Warp serials, spawn sequences, and deduplication windows use the same principle of recording an occurrence separately from its resulting value. For occurrences that carry payloads or require exactly-once presentation under resimulation, use the appropriate _then consequence, session event, Fire announcement, or simulation-lane tick payload event.
  • Spawn and resync values establish a baseline without firing edges. This includes interest re-entry and full snapshots. Put initial presentation in a typed <entity>_born hook or the Ev_Spawned event, which run after fields are applied. The census _spawned hook runs earlier for bookkeeping.
  • Host mutations use the same change comparison, so a hurt flash needs no is_host branch. A host-side pulse that ends within one network tick still does not reach clients; retain the changed state for a tick. The automatic edge pass runs inside session_tick. If the authority changes state after that frame's session update, its edge runs a frame late, which can matter when the callback moves an object read by the next simulation tick. With @(gd_step = "authority"), the generated <snake>_step(self, ticks) runs the authority loop and edge pass together in the same frame. For a manually driven loop, call ksess.session_run_edges(&ses) after the loop. Comparing and then committing the values makes this pass idempotent.
  • Edges run when the changed values are available. This is appropriate for scoreboards, hp, and inventories in row 4 of the two-timelines table. For spatial presentation that follows the render clock, such as a chest lid in row 2, call session_present inside the callback.
  • Edges report a state change, so two hits combined into one network delta produce one edge. When the number of occurrences or their arguments matter, use the simulation lane's mine-form _fx, a declared @(gd_event), or a command consequence.

Scriptgen permits _edge on reliable-delta fields and discrete owner fields. An edge on a predict field is a build error because resimulation would overwrite the change; use the mine-form _fx. An edge on an interpolated owner field is also a build error because the value interpolates every frame; derive presentation from the sampled fields instead. Use play/edge for local state that is not replicated.

Advanced: registry primitives#

Game code normally creates and removes entities through the generated Boot factory and typed <type>_* procedures. The engine-independent registry procedures underlying them are:

Odin
registry_spawn :: proc(reg: ^Registry, entity: rawptr, set: ^Command_Set, owner := PLAYER_ID_INVALID) -> Net_Id
registry_insert :: proc(reg: ^Registry, id: Net_Id, entity: rawptr, set: ^Command_Set, owner := PLAYER_ID_INVALID)
registry_remove :: proc(reg: ^Registry, id: Net_Id) -> bool
registry_get :: proc(reg: ^Registry, id: Net_Id) -> (^Registry_Entry, bool)
registry_teleport :: proc(reg: ^Registry, id: Net_Id)

The authority allocates ids with registry_spawn; remote peers mirror with registry_insert under the id from the wire (which also keeps next_id ahead so a migrated host keeps allocating without collisions). Net ids are never reused within a session. If Command_Set.net_id_offset is nonzero, the assigned id is written back into the entity's net_id field. registry_teleport declares a discontinuity in the entity's streamed fields. Every snapshot includes the warp counter, so receivers snap to the destination rather than interpolating across the map.

Game code normally keeps Net_Ref(T), a generic POD wrapper around Net_Id, instead of a raw pointer. The generated census constructs it with <entity>_ref and accepts it in <entity>_of; the resolver checks liveness and the declared entity kind before returning ^T. A replicated field such as target: knet.Net_Ref(Player) \gd:"replicate"`` therefore carries only the ID while preventing a Chest reference from being passed to a Player lookup at compile time. See Boot entity queries for typed owner queries and indexed iteration.

The per-tick walks#

Host deltas (reliable channel), and full snapshots for joins/backups:

Odin
registry_write_deltas :: proc(w: ^Writer, reg: ^Registry) -> int
registry_apply_deltas :: proc(r: ^Reader, reg: ^Registry, ctx: ^Command_Ctx = nil) -> int
registry_write_fulls :: proc(w: ^Writer, reg: ^Registry) -> int
registry_apply_fulls :: proc(r: ^Reader, reg: ^Registry, ctx: ^Command_Ctx = nil) -> int
registry_commit_shadows :: proc(reg: ^Registry)

Pass the client's ctx to the apply procs so entities with in-flight predictions get the unwind→apply→replay reconciliation; nil skips it (hosts, manually driven tests). After applying an authoritative full snapshot, call registry_commit_shadows so the next local diff doesn't re-flag everything.

Owner streams (unreliable channel), plus the once-per-frame sample:

Odin
registry_write_streams :: proc(w: ^Writer, reg: ^Registry, me: Player_Id, sender_now: f64) -> int
registry_stream_time :: proc(r: ^Reader) -> f64
registry_apply_streams :: proc(r: ^Reader, reg: ^Registry, me: Player_Id, stamp: f64) -> int
registry_sample_streams :: proc(reg: ^Registry, t: f64, me: Player_Id) -> int

Call registry_sample_streams once per frame (not per net tick) with t = timeline_now - interp_delay. Unknown ids in a stream batch are skipped by length rather than abandoning the batch; later ticks supply fresh samples.

Advanced: the command-loop primitives#

Issue gameplay commands through generated <verb>_cmd wrappers. The procedures below support custom session implementations and do not provide an alternate boolean API.

Odin
command_ctx_make :: proc(allocator := context.allocator) -> Command_Ctx
command_begin :: proc(ctx: ^Command_Ctx, entity: Net_Id, cmd: Cmd_Id)
command_issue :: proc(ctx: ^Command_Ctx, entity: rawptr, set: ^Command_Set, cmd: Cmd_Id) -> Command_Issue_Result
registry_host_command :: proc(reg: ^Registry, ctx: ^Command_Ctx, by: Player_Id, r: ^Reader, out: ^Writer, admission := Action_Reject_Reason.None) -> Registry_Command_Outcome
registry_client_result :: proc(reg: ^Registry, ctx: ^Command_Ctx, r: ^Reader, me := PLAYER_ID_INVALID) -> Command_Result
registry_expire_pending :: proc(reg: ^Registry, ctx: ^Command_Ctx, max_age_ticks: u64, me := PLAYER_ID_INVALID, out: ^[dynamic]Expired_Command = nil) -> int

The generated <proc>_cmd wrapper is the normal path (chest_take_cmd(&boot, chest, slot, px, py)), and kit/session installs the send hook and handles host execution, client results, and expiry. The command loop captures declared fields before execution and restores them on rejection on both peers, so a command returning false leaves no partial mutation in those fields. A locally rejected prediction is still sent: the client's copy may be stale, and the host decides whether to accept it. The host's per-peer Dedup_Window, a 64-command sliding window over intent sequences, prevents duplicate execution through retransmits and reconnect replays.

Typed app messages#

Use replicated fields for persistent state, a command for a requested mutation, and a presentation event for an effect. App messages serve transient communication: a whisper or emote directed to one peer, an out-of-band request/response, or a notification tied to no entity. They do not replay for peers that join later.

Declare an app-message handler with @(gd_message) and the SES_APP tag used to route it. The game assigns its tags around Kit's reserved routes: comms 0, xfer 2, and sim 3.

Odin
Whisper :: struct { spice: u16, emote, reserved: u8 } // canonical 4-byte payload
TAG_WHISPER :: u8(4)

@(gd_message = "TAG_WHISPER")
game_whisper :: proc(self: ^Game, from: knet.Player_Id, msg: Whisper) {
    // Decoded payload. The authority resolves `from`; clients receive
    // PLAYER_ID_INVALID. Perform sender-dependent validation on the authority.
}

Scriptgen generates the route, a game_messages(self, &ses) registration procedure to call once in ready() like fire_listen, and two send procedures:

Odin
game_whisper_send(&ses, msg, ksess.HOST_PEER)   // to a peer, or ksess.BROADCAST_PEER
game_whisper_send_to(&ses, player, msg)         // to a player; the host resolves its seat

It wraps the runtime typed-route API (session_app_send_typed / session_app_listen), which remains available for custom routing. The generated payload has a canonical raw ABI: fixed-width, recursively validated, padding-free bytes. Frame strings and other variable data yourself on a bare session_app_route. The full field layout enters NET_FINGERPRINT, so peers reject a join when the builds disagree on the payload layout or another part of the wire schema. The declared tag must resolve to a package-level byte literal such as TAG_WHISPER :: u8(4); its numeric route, not only the identifier, enters the schema. Cavecrawl's arrival greeting is an example.

A message saying "Player X's score is now 5" does not supply that score to a peer who joins a second later. A dropped packet can also lose the update if the message uses unreliable delivery. Replicate the score so a snapshot can restore its current value. Reserve messages for signals addressed to peers that are listening when they are sent.

Wire, tick, and clocks#

Writer/Reader are a bounds-checked, little-endian, append/cursor pair: fixed-width fields, u16-length strings, no varints. The error model: a Reader that runs past its data sets a sticky err and returns zero values from then on, so callers check r.err once after a decode block. A malformed packet can never read out of bounds or panic, since remote input is untrusted by default. read_string/read_bytes return zero-copy views into the packet; clone anything you keep.

Length prefixes describe the encoding; admission limits bound the work a decoder can perform before looping, cloning data, or calling game code:

Envelope Ceiling
Session packet (MAX_PACKET_BYTES) 1 MiB
One length-prefixed string/byte field (MAX_FIELD_BYTES) 65,535 B
One counted container (MAX_CONTAINER_ITEMS) 4,096 rows, within the packet ceiling
One replicated field / complete entity row 65,535 B
Command arguments 4 KiB by default; at most 65,535 B with an explicit policy
Profile row 256 B
App message / entity blob 256 KiB
Simulation event tuple (SIM_FACT wire frame) 4 KiB

Outgoing session packets pass the same checks, so the authority cannot send a packet every receiver would reject. Delta and stream batches stop before the packet ceiling and leave unsent shadows dirty for a later tick. Use kit/xfer for bulk assets; its 8 KiB chunks remain ordinary bounded messages. read_string_limited and read_bytes_limited let a subsystem choose a tighter semantic bound than the shared field maximum.

Odin
now_s :: proc "contextless" () -> f64            // monotonic seconds
ticker_make :: proc(hz := DEFAULT_TICK_HZ) -> Ticker
ticker_advance :: proc(t: ^Ticker, frame_dt: f64) -> int
clock_sample :: proc(c: ^Clock_Sync, local_send, remote_time, local_recv: f64)
clock_remote_now :: proc(c: ^Clock_Sync, local_now: f64) -> f64
interp_render_time :: proc(c: ^Clock_Sync, local_now: f64, delay: f64) -> f64

ticker_advance returns the number of network ticks due this frame, capped at eight so a long stall does not produce an unbounded catch-up burst. Clock_Sync uses an exponentially weighted moving average over ping samples. It feeds owner stream interpolation and the session's ping stat; it does not model long-term clock drift. The clock also records smoothed RTT deviation as jitter. Read the per-peer value with session_clock for diagnostics or connection-quality UI.

The two timelines (presenting consequences)#

A peer displaying a remote owner stream uses two timelines:

  • Wire time: reliable deltas, entity lifetime, and command results apply when their ordered messages arrive.
  • Render time: remote owner-streamed fields are displayed at interp_delay, providing a buffer for interpolation.

This difference matters when reliable state is the consequence of remote movement. Applying a door-open animation immediately can make the door appear to open before the delayed remote player reaches it. Apply authoritative state immediately, but schedule spatial presentation with the cause when appropriate.

session_present selects immediate or delayed presentation from one decision only the game knows: whether the local player's simulation caused the effect.

Odin
ksess.session_present(
	&game.ses,
	id == game.my_claim,
	game,
	present_gem_gone,
	id,
)

present_gem_gone :: proc(user: rawptr, id: knet.Net_Id, a: u64) {
	// hide, burst, sound
}

When mine is true, the callback runs immediately. Otherwise it runs on the remote render clock. knet.Later is the lower-level scheduler used by this helper.

An entity or visual state needed by a delayed effect must remain available until the effect can run. Use a despawn dwell or session_present's extra delay with a reaper callback when necessary.

Choose a presentation method according to the consequence's cause:

The consequence's cause Present it The tool
Local owner simulation (a local claim or strike) now session_present(mine = true), or present directly
A remote moving cause (a streamed avatar/ball reaching a thing) at the render clock session_present(mine = false)
A per-peer local visual (each screen flies its own projectile) at my visual's moment fx hooks (kit/fx On_Hit_Proc)
No spatial cause (scoreboards, inventories, objectives) on arrival a <field>_edge half
A global transition (the won byte, the hole index) after a dwell edge-outlives-observers: hold state ≥ interp_delay

Classify each consequence independently. A looted chest can update the inventory UI immediately while delaying the lid animation to match a remote player's rendered interaction.

Reducing interp_delay or increasing tick_hz through session_configure reduces presentation delay but leaves less buffer for jitter. First align effects with their causes. A delay chosen for a LAN can leave a 120ms link without a newer motion sample to interpolate toward; a delay chosen for that link can make LAN presentation unnecessarily late.

cfg.interp_adapt, off by default, adjusts toward the delay required by the worst active link: rtt/2 + 2·jitter, using the same clock data as the ping stat. It grows promptly for headroom and shrinks slowly with hysteresis. The configured interp_delay becomes the floor, and session_interp_target returns the target delay.

Game-controlled presentation clocks#

For row 3, where each screen moves its own projectile, the game must schedule effects on the projectile's clock. session_present(mine=false) delays its callback by interp_delay to align with a cause rendered through the interpolated stream. That alignment is correct only when the cause uses the interpolated timeline; session_present cannot check this condition.

An entity the game already renders at now - interp_delay is already delayed. Passing its hit or splash through session_present(mine = false) delays the effect a second time. When the game owns the cause's clock, carry a timestamp and present the consequence on that clock. Use session_present for causes whose delayed rendering is owned by Kit's owner-stream interpolation.

Projectiles: put a clock in the spawn tuple#

If a projectile replicates only a spawn tuple ({origin, dir, speed}), each peer may start integrating motion when its packet arrives. That makes the local spawn time depend on packet transit. The resulting position offset persists for the projectile's lifetime: peers with different latency display the same bullet in different places, and projectiles spawned in one host frame can appear tens of ms apart.

Include time in the tuple and evaluate position from it:

  1. Add the host's world-time at spawn (Birth) and a DeadAt timestamp, producing 5 fields rather than 3. Evaluate pos(t) = origin + dir·speed·(t − Birth) instead of integrating from arrival.
  2. Render at now - interp_delay to match the time used for other remote entities. Drawing the projectile at host-now while drawing its target in the past can make it appear to pass through a target that has not visibly reacted.
  3. Remove the projectile at DeadAt on that clock. Do not add another delay through session_present.
  4. For a bounce, replicate a new origin/dir/Birth tuple and a segment counter. Use the counter's edge for the bounce sound. Replicating the current segment lets a late joiner reconstruct it; a transient bounce event alone would leave that peer on the original segment.

A live projectile needs no continuous motion updates once peers have its tuple. Spawn bursts dominate traffic in this model, so batch spawns when their volume becomes a problem. Interest management and f16 packing do not reduce the number of spawn operations.

A cosmetic row-3 visual can use a less precise clock. Cavecrawl's rock tracer (kit/fx tracer_add) integrates a spawn tuple from arrival and draws at now. The host keeps the damaging rock in its local flying array and tests hits there. A Fire announcement creates the visual; accepted damage reaches peers through replicated hp. The rock itself is not a replicated entity, and tracer positions can differ between peers. Use birth timestamps when a peer relies on the projectile's position to judge a hit, dodge, or block.

Shared replication and simulation primitives#

kit/net provides the wire format, field descriptors and codecs, interpolation math, ticks, and clocks used by both session replication and kit/sim. Session replication adds commands and owner streams on top of those shared primitives. kit/sim adds server-authoritative simulation and resimulation in a separate package. Its documentation calls the shared primitives the substrate layer of kit/net. Field_Desc also carries simulation-only tuning fields (slack, glide, cut) that only the simulation lane reads.

Three related names refer to different presentation operations. session_present queues one consequence for the render clock; see the two timelines. lane_present runs kit/sim's per-frame presentation update for watched and reconciled entities. kit/sim/present.odin implements the blending and error-correction math used by that update.

Constraints and failure cases#

  • A client write to an authority-owned field, such as self.score += 1, changes the local value without replicating it. The write guard compares each client's reliable-delta fields with the values last applied by the framework once per network tick. It reports the class, field, and required fix: issue a command or compute the value on the authority. Pending cooperative predictions and simulation commands are exempt, so permitted optimistic writes do not trigger the guard. Scriptgen also rejects direct calls to @(gd_command) procedures and points to the <verb>_cmd wrapper. It diagnoses gd-shaped tags under a misspelled namespace, such as gs:"replicate", rather than ignoring them. Development builds assert on a violation. Under -disable-assert, the session retains the comparison and increments session_guard_hits; native builds also log the first violation. See session.
  • Deltas compare entity bytes with their shadow once per network tick. A byte pulsed 1 → 0 within one tick can equal its shadow when the comparison runs, so no change is sent. Hold state for at least a tick, as cavecrawl does with level.won staying 1 until the next run, or use an explicit reliable message. A <field>_edge half reacts to received changes; it cannot recover a pulse that replication did not send.
  • Owner-streamed fields are never written by network input on the owner's peer. registry_apply_streams skips entities owned by me; reject-truth, prediction reverts, and expiry all pass skip_owner for them; diff_mask keeps them out of deltas entirely. This prevents a rejected cast from moving the entity owner back to the host's older position sample. Full snapshots at join or world seeding do write these fields to establish their initial values.
  • registry_get returns a pointer into the registry, so mutations land in place with no store-back required. It stays valid only until the next insert/remove. Don't hold it across a spawn.
  • Reliable channel ordering is required. A delta that already contains a command's effect must arrive after that command's result, and a delta batch must never name an id the peer hasn't seen spawn (an unknown id abandons the batch: field sizes come from the descriptor the peer doesn't have). The session guarantees both by putting results, state batches, and spawn/despawn on the same reliable ordered channel.
  • Canonical fixed-shape values only, 64 fields max. scriptgen recursively rejects platform-width leaves, implicit enum widths, pointers, unsupported containers, and hidden interior or tail padding, naming the complete field path. Generated target-side layout assertions are a second check. Group past-64 field counts into sub-structs (a fixed array is one field).
  • Intent_Seq wraparound is not handled: u32 gives ~4 billion commands per peer per session.

See also: kit/session (drives all of this), kit/netgd (transport), kit/sim (the server-authority resim lane beside these two, which timelines helps you choose), kit/comms, kit/combat, kit/save.
